Content:
Recall that the principal components of a standardized observation matrix [MATH: X] are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.] If

Content:
[MATH: \lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n]

Content:
are the eigenvalues of [MATH: C] written in descending order, then:

Content:
- the [MATH: 1]st principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf u_1] corresponding to the [MATH: 1]st eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_1,]
- the [MATH: 2]nd principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf u_2] corresponding to the [MATH: 2]nd eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2,]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Content:
and so on.

Content:
For example, suppose that the covariance matrix [MATH: C] of some particular observations is

Content:
[MATH: [9|1; 1|9]]

Content:
It's easy to show that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix [MATH: C,] in descending order, are

Content:
[MATH: \lambda_1=10, \qquad
\lambda_2=8.]

Content:
To find the first principal component of the data, we need the unit eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_1=10.]

Content:
Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

Content:
[MATH: C − 10I|= [9|1; 1|9] − 10[1|0; 0|1] = [− 1|1; 1|− 1].]

Content:
Now, seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (C-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector

Content:
[MATH: [1; 1]]

Content:
Finally, dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},] we get

Content:
[MATH: [1; 1]]

Content:
Therefore, the [MATH: 1]st principal component of the data is [MATH: [1; 1]]

Content:
Note: The opposite vector [MATH: [1; 1]] also works in the example above.

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [MATH: C] are called the principal components of the data. If

[MATH: \lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n]

are the eigenvalues of [MATH: C] written in descending order, then:

  • the [MATH: 1]st principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf u_1] corresponding to the [MATH: 1]st eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_1,]

  • the [MATH: 2]nd principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf u_2] corresponding to the [MATH: 2]nd eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2,]

  • [MATH: \cdots]

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix [MATH: C,] in descending order, are [MATH: \lambda_1=16] and [MATH: \lambda_2=6.] So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2=6{:}]

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

[MATH: C − 6I|= [7|3; 3|15] − 6[1|0; 0|1] = [1|3; 3|9].]

Seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (C-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector [MATH: [− 3; 1]]

Finally, dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{10},] we get

[MATH: [− 3; 1]]

Therefore, the second principal component of the data is [MATH: [− 3; 1]]
